summary: Defines a metric for the round-trip delay of packets across Internet paths, which is the time for a packet to go out and the reply to come back.

plainLanguage.summary: This document says exactly how to measure how long a packet takes to reach a host and for the reply to come back, and how to report the number so that two different measuring tools give results you can compare. It also says how much of the number is the measurement's own fault.

questions: what is a poisson stream in ippm
subtitle: A precise definition of how to measure the time a packet takes to reach a host and for the reply to return.

tldr.problem: A round-trip delay measurement is easy to run but easy to report badly, because clock errors, the destination's own processing time and the choice of test packet all change the number.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a singleton metric, Type-P-Round-trip-Delay, measured from the first bit leaving the source interface to the last bit of the reply arriving back, then a Poisson-scheduled sample of those singletons and four statistics over the sample.
tldr.outcome: Two implementations that follow the definition produce comparable numbers, because the calibration error, the loss threshold and the Type-P of the test packets must all be reported alongside the values.

today: RFC 2681 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the round-trip companion to the one-way delay metric in RFC 2679, and both build on the IP Performance Metrics framework in RFC 2330.

sections.title: Why Measure the Round Trip
sections.content:
Round-trip delay of a Type-P packet from a source host to a destination host is useful for several reasons. Some applications do not perform well, or at all, if the end-to-end delay between hosts is large relative to some threshold value. Erratic variation in delay makes it difficult, or impossible, to support many interactive real-time applications. The larger the value of delay, the more difficult it is for transport-layer protocols to sustain high bandwidths. The minimum value of this metric gives an indication of the delay due only to propagation and transmission delay, and of the delay that will likely be experienced when the path is lightly loaded. Values above the minimum give an indication of the congestion present in the path.

Measuring round-trip delay instead of one-way delay has several weaknesses. The Internet path from a source to a destination may differ from the path back, so that different sequences of routers are used in each direction, and round-trip measurements then measure the performance of two distinct paths together. Even when the two paths are symmetric, they may have radically different performance characteristics because of asymmetric queueing. The performance of an application may depend mostly on the performance in one direction. And in quality-of-service enabled networks, provisioning in one direction may be radically different from provisioning in the reverse direction, so the QoS guarantees differ.

The measurement of round-trip delay has two specific advantages. The first is ease of deployment: unlike one-way measurement, it is often possible to perform some form of round-trip delay measurement without installing measurement-specific software at the intended destination. A variety of approaches are well known, including the use of ICMP Echo or of TCP-based methodologies. The second is ease of interpretation: in some circumstances the round-trip time is in fact the quantity of interest, and deducing it from matching one-way measurements plus an assumption about destination processing time is less direct and potentially less accurate.
sections.plainLanguage: Some applications need a reply quickly, and a network that is busy makes the reply slow. Measuring the round trip is easier to deploy than measuring each direction separately, because the destination often needs no special software. The cost is that the two directions are lumped together.

sections.title: Four Ways a Clock Can Be Wrong
sections.content:
Whenever a time is mentioned in this document it is understood to be measured in seconds, and fractions of seconds, relative to UTC. The Framework document describes four distinct but related notions of clock uncertainty.

  • Synchronization measures the extent to which two clocks agree on what time it is. For example, the clock on one host might be 5.4 msec ahead of the clock on a second host.
  • Accuracy measures the extent to which a given clock agrees with UTC. For example, the clock on a host might be 27.1 msec behind UTC.
  • Resolution measures the precision of a given clock. For example, the clock on an old Unix host might tick only once every 10 msec, and thus have a resolution of only 10 msec.
  • Skew measures the change of accuracy, or of synchronization, with time. For example, the clock on a given host might gain 1.3 msec per hour and thus be 27.1 msec behind UTC at one time and only 25.8 msec an hour later.

The document tags a technical term from the Framework document with a trailing asterisk the first time it is used, so that "term*" indicates that the term is defined in the Framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Four different things can make a clock wrong, and they matter in different ways: two clocks can disagree, a clock can be off from real time, a clock may be coarse, or a clock may drift. The document keeps them apart because a delay measurement is affected by them differently.

sections.title: The Singleton Metric
sections.content:
The metric is named Type-P-Round-trip-Delay. Its parameters are Src, the IP address of a host, Dst, the IP address of a host, and T, a time. Its value is either a real number, or an undefined, informally infinite, number of seconds.

The definition is precise. The Type-P-Round-trip-Delay from Src to Dst at T is dT means that Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T, that Dst received that packet, then immediately sent a Type-P packet back to Src, and that Src received the last bit of that packet at wire-time T+dT.

The metric is undefined, informally infinite, means that Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T and that either Dst did not receive the packet, Dst did not send a Type-P packet in response, or Src did not receive that response packet. The round-trip delay between Src and Dst at T means either the delay from Src to Dst at T or the delay from Dst to Src at T; when this notion is used it is understood to be specifically ambiguous which host acts as Src and which as Dst. The document notes that this ambiguity will usually be a small price to pay for being able to have one measurement, launched from either Src or Dst, rather than having two measurements.

Several issues are likely to come up in practice. The timestamp values should be fairly accurate in order to draw meaningful conclusions about the state of the network at a given T, so Src should have an accurate knowledge of time of day. NTP affords one way to achieve time accuracy to within several milliseconds, and higher accuracy may be achieved when NTP servers use GPS systems as a time source. NTP will adjust the instrument's clock, and if an adjustment is made between the time the initial timestamp is taken and the time the final timestamp is taken, that adjustment affects the uncertainty in the measured delay and must be accounted for in the instrument's calibration.

A given methodology has to include a way to determine whether a delay value is infinite or merely very large, with the packet yet to arrive at Dst. Simple upper bounds, such as the 255 seconds theoretical upper bound on the lifetimes of IP packets, could be used, but good engineering and an understanding of packet lifetimes are needed in practice. If the packet is duplicated so that multiple non-corrupt instances of the response arrive back at the source, the packet is counted as received, and the first instance to arrive determines the packet's round-trip delay. If the packet is fragmented and reassembly does not occur, the packet is deemed lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurement starts when the first bit of the test packet leaves the sending machine's network card and stops when the last bit of the reply comes back in. If no reply comes back, the delay counts as infinite rather than as some large number.

sections.title: How to Measure It
sections.content:
As with other Type-P metrics, the detailed methodology depends on the Type-P, for example the protocol number, the UDP or TCP port number, the size and the precedence. For a given Type-P, the methodology proceeds as follows.

At the source host, select the Src and Dst IP addresses and form a test packet of Type-P with these addresses. Any padding portion of the packet needed only to make the test packet a given size should be filled with randomized bits, to avoid a situation in which the measured delay is lower than it would otherwise be because of compression techniques along the path. The test packet must have some identifying information so that the response can be identified when it arrives; one way to do this is to place the timestamp generated just before sending the test packet in the packet itself.

At the destination host, arrange to receive and respond to the test packet. At the source host, arrange to receive the corresponding response packet.

At the source host, take the initial timestamp and then send the prepared Type-P packet towards the destination. The timestamp could be placed inside the packet, or kept separately as long as the packet contains a suitable identifier so that the received timestamp can be compared with the send timestamp.

If the packet arrives at the destination, send a corresponding response packet back as soon as possible. If the response packet arrives within a reasonable period of time, take the final timestamp as soon as possible upon receipt. Subtracting the two timestamps gives an estimate of round-trip delay. If the delay between the initial timestamp and the actual sending of the packet is known, the estimate can be adjusted by subtracting that amount, and the uncertainty in that value must be taken into account in the error analysis. The same applies to the delay between the actual receipt of the response packet and the final timestamp.

If the packet fails to arrive within a reasonable period of time, the round-trip delay is taken to be undefined, informally infinite. The threshold of reasonable is a parameter of the methodology. Issues such as the packet format and the means by which the destination knows when to expect the test packet are outside the scope of the document.

The document adds two notes. You cannot in general add two one-way delay values to form a round-trip delay value, because the return packet must be triggered by the reception of a packet from the source. And "ping" would qualify as a round-trip measure under this definition, with a Type-P of ICMP echo request and reply with 60-byte packets, but the uncertainties associated with a typical ping program must be analyzed, including the type of reflecting point, since a router may not handle an ICMP request in the fast path, and the effects of load on the reflecting point.
sections.plainLanguage: Send a test packet with a timestamp in it, reply as fast as you can when it arrives, and subtract the two timestamps. Fill any padding with random bits so that compression on the path does not make the packet look smaller than it is.

sections.title: Where the Error Comes From
sections.content:
The description of any specific measurement method should account for sources of error or uncertainty. Three are noted for delay metrics: uncertainty in the clock of the source host, the difference between wire time and host time, and the time required by the destination to receive the packet and send the response. The loss threshold may also affect the results.

On clocks, the uncertainty is related to uncertainty in the source clock. The clock used to measure when the packet was sent is called the source clock, the observed send time is Tinitial and the observed receive time is Tfinal. In one-way delay there is an issue of synchronizing the source and destination clocks, while in round-trip delay there is an easier issue of self-synchronization between the source clock when the test packet is sent and the same source clock when the response arrives. The greater practical threat is anything that causes a discontinuity in the source clock between the two timestamps, which might happen with certain implementations of NTP. The accuracy of a clock matters only in identifying the time at which a delay was measured, not for the accuracy of the measurement itself. The resolution of a clock adds to uncertainty about any time measured with it, so a source clock with a resolution of 10 msec adds 10 msec of uncertainty to any time value measured with it; this resolution is denoted Rsource. Naive computation of Tfinal minus Tinitial is therefore off by 2*Rsource.

On wire time against host time, the metric would like to measure the time between when the test packet leaves the network interface of the source and when the response packet completely arrives there. Software on the source can only directly measure the time between grabbing a timestamp just prior to sending and grabbing one just after receiving, and these are host times. Hinitial is an upper bound on the uncertainty in the difference between wire time and host time when sending, and Hfinal is the same for receiving, and these introduce a total uncertainty of Hinitial + Hfinal.

On the destination producing a response, any time it spends receiving and recognizing the packet and then producing and sending the response adds further error. The error equals the difference between the wire time the first bit of the packet is received and the wire time the first bit of the response is sent, and the uncertainty in that difference is denoted Hrefl.

Calibration decomposes measured values as measured value equals true value plus systematic error plus random error. If the systematic error can be determined it can be compensated for, leaving reported value equals true value plus random error. At a minimum, a bound should be found such that the reported value is in the range of true value minus e to true value plus e at least 95 percent of the time; e is the calibration error, and it represents the degree to which the values produced by the measurement instrument are repeatable. The error in measurements could be bounded by adding up all the individual uncertainties, giving 2*Rsource + Hinitial + Hfinal + Hrefl.

Reasonable bounds on both the clock-related uncertainty and the host-related uncertainty should be possible by careful design and by calibrating the instruments using a known, isolated network in a lab. The host-related uncertainties could be bounded by connecting two instruments back to back with a high-speed serial link or isolated LAN segment, so that repeated measurements measure the same round-trip delay. If the test packets are small, such a connection has a minimal delay that may be approximated by zero, so the measured delay contains only systematic and random error in the instrumentation; the average value of repeated measurements is the systematic error and the variation is the random error. One way to compute the systematic error, and the random error to a 95 percent confidence, is to repeat the experiment many times, at least hundreds of tests. The systematic error would then be the median, and the random error could be found by removing the systematic error from the measured values. The 95 percent confidence interval would be the range from the 2.5th percentile to the 97.5th percentile of these deviations, and the calibration error e could be taken as the largest absolute value of these two numbers, plus the clock-related uncertainty.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things make the number wrong: the clock, the gap between the moment a packet reaches the card and the moment the software stamps it, and the time the far end spends replying. The document gives an error budget for all three and a way to measure the instrument's own error in a lab.

sections.title: A Sample of Delays
sections.content:
Given the singleton metric, the document defines one particular sample of such singletons. The idea of the sample is to select a particular binding of the parameters Src, Dst and Type-P, then define a sample of values of the parameter T. The means for defining the values of T is to select a beginning time T0, a final time Tf, and an average rate lambda, then define a pseudo-random Poisson process of rate lambda whose values fall between T0 and Tf. The time interval between successive values of T will then average 1/lambda.

The sample is named Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Poisson-Stream. Its parameters are Src, Dst, T0, Tf and lambda, where lambda is a rate in reciprocal seconds. Its units are a sequence of pairs, where the elements of each pair are a time T and a value dT that is either a real number or an undefined number of seconds. The values of T in the sequence are monotonically increasing.

The definition: given T0, Tf and lambda, compute a pseudo-random Poisson process beginning at or before T0, with average arrival rate lambda, and ending at or after Tf. Those time values greater than or equal to T0 and less than or equal to Tf are then selected. At each of the times in this process, the value of Type-P-Round-trip-Delay at that time is obtained. The value of the sample is the sequence made up of the resulting time and delay pairs. If there are no such pairs, the sequence is of length zero and the sample is said to be empty.

The value of lambda is not constrained, except to note the extremes: if the rate is too large, the measurement traffic will perturb the network and itself cause congestion, while if the rate is too small, interesting network behaviour might not be captured. Since a pseudo-random number sequence is employed, the sequence of times, and hence the value of the sample, is not fully specified, and pseudo-random number generators of good quality will be needed. The sample is defined in terms of a Poisson process both to avoid the effects of self-synchronization and to capture a sample that is statistically as unbiased as possible. The Poisson process is used to schedule the delay measurements; the test packets will generally not arrive at the destination according to a Poisson distribution, nor will response packets arrive at the source according to one, since they are influenced by the network.

The methodologies follow directly from the selection of specific times using the specified Poisson arrival process and from the methodologies already given for the singleton metric. Care must be given to correctly handle out-of-order arrival of test or response packets: it is possible that the source sends one test packet at one time, then a second test packet later, and receives the second response first and the first response later.

The calibration and context for the underlying singletons MUST be reported along with the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one measurement, the document defines a set of them taken at random times, spaced on average by one over the chosen rate. Random spacing avoids lining the tests up with regular patterns in the traffic.

sections.title: Statistics Over the Sample
sections.content:
Four statistics are offered, mostly to be illustrative of what could be done.

Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Percentile is, given a stream and a percent X between 0 percent and 100 percent, the Xth percentile of all the dT values in the stream. Undefined values are treated as infinitely large, so the percentile could itself be undefined. It is undefined if the sample is empty. The worked example uses a stream of 100 msec, 110 msec, undefined, 90 msec and 500 msec, where the 50th percentile is 110 msec, since 90 msec and 100 msec are smaller while 110 msec and undefined are larger. If the possibility that a packet with finite delay is reported as lost is significant, then a high percentile, the 90th or 95th, might be reported as infinite instead of finite.

Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Median is the median of all the dT values, with undefined values treated as infinitely large, and it is undefined if the sample is empty. The median differs from the 50th percentile only when the sample contains an even number of values, in which case the mean of the two central values is used. In an example stream of 100, 110, undefined and 90 msec, the median is 105 msec, the mean of 100 and 110.

Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Minimum is the minimum of all the dT values, with undefined values treated as infinitely large, so it could be undefined if all values are undefined, and it is undefined if the sample is empty. In the first example the minimum is 90 msec.

Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Inverse-Percentile is, given a stream and a time duration threshold, the fraction of all the dT values in the stream less than or equal to the threshold. The result could be as low as 0 percent, if all the dT values exceed the threshold, or as high as 100 percent, and it is undefined if the sample is empty. In the first example, the Inverse-Percentile of 103 msec is 50 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: Four ways of summarising a set of delay measurements: a chosen percentile, the middle value, the smallest value, and the share of measurements below a threshold. A measurement with no reply counts as infinitely slow in all four.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conducting Internet measurements raises both security and privacy concerns. This memo does not specify an implementation of the metrics, so it does not directly affect the security of the Internet nor of applications which run on it. Implementations of the metrics must nonetheless be mindful of security and privacy concerns.

There are two types of security concern: potential harm caused by the measurements, and potential harm to the measurements. The measurements could cause harm because they are active and inject packets into the network. The measurement parameters MUST be carefully selected so that the measurements inject trivial amounts of additional traffic into the networks they measure. If they inject too much traffic they can skew the results of the measurement and, in extreme cases, cause congestion and denial of service.

The measurements themselves could be harmed by routers giving measurement traffic a different priority than normal traffic, or by an attacker injecting artificial measurement traffic. If routers can recognize measurement traffic and treat it separately, the measurements will not reflect actual user traffic. If an attacker injects artificial traffic that is accepted as legitimate, the loss rate will be artificially lowered. The measurement methodologies SHOULD therefore include appropriate techniques to reduce the probability that measurement traffic can be distinguished from normal traffic, and authentication techniques such as digital signatures may be used where appropriate to guard against injected traffic attacks.

The privacy concerns of network measurement are limited by the active measurements described in this memo. Unlike passive measurements, there can be no release of existing user data.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring puts real packets into the network, so the tests must be light enough not to distort what they are measuring. And the tests can be fooled: an attacker sending fake replies would make the loss rate look better than it is.

messages.label: Type-P test packet
messages.note: Sent at wire-time T; carries a timestamp or an identifier.

messages.label: Type-P response packet
messages.note: Sent immediately on arrival; the time spent here is Hrefl.

messages.label: Tfinal - Tinitial
messages.note: The round-trip delay dT, off by 2*Rsource.

viz.caption: THE FOUR NOTIONS OF CLOCK UNCERTAINTY (SECTION 1.2)

items.title: Synchronization
items.text: How far two clocks disagree about the time. One host's clock might be 5.4 msec ahead of another's.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: How far one clock is from UTC. A host's clock might be 27.1 msec behind UTC.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: How finely a clock ticks. An old Unix host might tick only once every 10 msec.

items.title: Skew
items.text: How the accuracy drifts over time. A clock might gain 1.3 msec per hour.

items.title: 2*Rsource
items.text: Twice the resolution of the source clock, because the naive subtraction of the two timestamps is off by that much.

items.title: Hinitial
items.text: Uncertainty in the gap between wire time and host time when the test packet is sent.

items.title: Hfinal
items.text: Uncertainty in the gap between wire time and host time when the response is received.

items.title: Hrefl
items.text: Uncertainty in the time the destination spends between receiving the packet and sending the response.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STATISTICS OVER A SAMPLE (SECTION 4)

items.label: Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Percentile
items.desc: The Xth percentile of all the delay values, with undefined values treated as infinitely large.

items.label: Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Median
items.desc: The median of all the delay values, with undefined values treated as infinitely large.

items.label: Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Minimum
items.desc: The smallest of all the delay values, with undefined values treated as infinitely large.

items.label: Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Inverse-Percentile
items.desc: The fraction of the delay values less than or equal to a given threshold, from 0 to 100 percent.
